noteRef.topicTitle: The nature and variety of living organisms

specPoints.text: describe the common features shown by eukaryotic organisms: plants, animals, fungi and protoctists Plants: these are multicellular organisms; their cells contain chloroplasts and are able to carry out photosynthesis; their cells have cellulose cell walls; they store carbohydrates as starch or sucrose. Examples include flowering plants, such as a cereal (for example, maize), and a herbaceous legume (for example, peas or beans). Animals: these are multicellular organisms; their cells do not contain chloroplasts and are not able to carry out photosynthesis; they have no cell walls; they usually have nervous co-ordination and are able to move from one place to another; they often store carbohydrate as glycogen. Examples include mammals (for example, humans) and insects (for example, housefly and mosquito). Fungi: these are organisms that are not able to carry out photosynthesis; their body is usually organised into a mycelium made from thread-like structures called hyphae, which contain many nuclei; some examples are single-celled; their cells have walls made of chitin; they feed by extracellular secretion of digestive enzymes onto food material and absorption of the organic products; this is known as saprotrophic nutrition; they may store carbohydrate as glycogen. Examples include Mucor , which has the typical fungal hyphal structure, and yeast, which is single-celled. Protoctists: these are microscopic single-celled organisms. Some, like Amoeba , that live in pond water, have features like an animal cell, while others, like Chlorella , have chloroplasts and are more like plants. A pathogenic example is Plasmodium , responsible for causing malaria.

primer.text: Eukaryotes are the organisms whose cells keep their DNA inside a nucleus surrounded by its own membrane. This note tours the four groups you must know — animals, plants, fungi and protoctists — and pins down the features that examiners expect you to list for each one, plus the drawings you should be able to interpret.

lessons.title: The eukaryotic cell plan: one shared blueprint
sourceHeadings: Common Features of Eukaryotic Organisms: Basics
lessons.opening: Every organism whose cells store DNA inside a membrane-bound nucleus counts as a eukaryote. That single design feature splits the living world into two camps, because prokaryotes keep their genetic material loose in the cytoplasm. Some eukaryotes build bodies made of many cells, while others live as a single cell, yet both forms belong here.
keyPoints: A eukaryotic cell keeps its chromosome inside a nucleus that has its own surrounding membrane.
The four eukaryote groups named in this course are animals, plants, fungi and protoctists.
Being eukaryotic does not fix body size: members can be built from many cells or just one.
Under a light microscope the shared nucleus with its surrounding membrane marks both animal and plant cells as eukaryotic.

low.restatement: Eukaryotes are the organisms whose cells have a nucleus enclosed by a membrane; the four groups to remember are animals, plants, fungi and protoctists.
low.analogy: Picture the nucleus as a locked office holding all the paperwork, while prokaryotes leave theirs on an open desk in the middle of the room.
low.examPointer: If a question hands you a micrograph, find the dark round shape ringed by a double line — that visible enclosed nucleus is your evidence for calling the cell eukaryotic.

medium.restatement: The membrane around the nucleus separates transcription from translation and is the universal eukaryotic signature; body design (one cell or many) is a separate, independent variable.
medium.analogy: Two houses can look completely different outside yet share identical wiring behind the walls — body plan varies, the enclosed-nucleus wiring never does.
medium.examPointer: Comparisons between eukaryotes and prokaryotes earn marks only if the nucleus (or its absence) is stated explicitly, so lead with it before any other feature.

check.stem: Which feature is shared by every eukaryotic organism?

options.text: Their DNA sits inside a nucleus enclosed by its own membrane
options.explanation: This is the universal eukaryotic signature named in the note.

options.text: Their cells always contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis
options.explanation: Fungi and animals never photosynthesise, so this cannot be universal.

options.text: They are always built from many cooperating cells
options.explanation: Yeasts and many protoctists live as single cells, so multicellularity is not shared.

options.text: Their genetic material floats freely in the cytoplasm
options.explanation: That describes prokaryotes, the group the note contrasts against eukaryotes.

check.stem: Which list contains only eukaryotic groups?

options.text: Protoctists, animals, bacteria, plants
options.explanation: Again bacteria sneak in; the fourth slot should be fungi.

options.text: Animals, plants, fungi, protoctists
options.explanation: These are exactly the four eukaryote groups the note names.

options.text: Animals, plants, bacteria, fungi
options.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotic, so the list mixes the two camps.

options.text: Plants, fungi, protoctists, viruses
options.explanation: Viruses sit outside the classification of living organisms altogether.
options.misconception: viruses misfiled as a eukaryote group

check.stem: A single-celled organism is found to have a membrane-enclosed nucleus. How should it be classified?

options.text: A virus, because it has so few parts
options.explanation: Viruses have no cellular structure at all, let alone a nucleus.
options.misconception: virus treated as a small cell

options.text: Neither group, because classification needs multicellularity
options.explanation: Nothing in the classification demands many cells.

options.text: A eukaryote, because body size does not change the cell plan
options.explanation: Single-celled eukaryotes exist, so the nucleus decides the group.

options.text: A prokaryote, because all single cells are prokaryotic
options.explanation: Plenty of protoctists and yeasts are single cells with enclosed nuclei.

check.stem: Under a light microscope, which observation most directly supports calling a cell eukaryotic?

options.text: The cell has a regular rectangular outline
options.explanation: Shape tells you about the wall, not about DNA packaging.
options.misconception: cell shape used as nuclear evidence

options.text: The specimen moves across the field of view
options.explanation: Movement is a life process, not a cell-plan feature.

options.text: The cell stains darker at its edges than at its centre
options.explanation: Edge staining says nothing reliable about the nucleus.

options.text: A dark rounded region enclosed by a distinct membrane is visible
options.explanation: That is the nucleus, the deciding eukaryotic feature.

check.stem: Why can body design never settle whether an organism is eukaryotic?

options.text: Because eukaryotes and prokaryotes each include both single-celled and many-celled members
options.explanation: The note states eukaryotes may be single-celled or multicellular, so body design cuts across both camps.

options.text: Because every living thing is made of exactly one cell
options.explanation: Animals and plants are obviously many-celled.

options.text: Because only organisms with cell walls can be many-celled
options.explanation: Animal cells lack walls yet build whole bodies.

options.text: Because microscopes cannot resolve whether a body has one cell
options.explanation: Cell count is exactly what microscopy resolves well.

check.stem: State the shared cell feature that defines the eukaryote camp.
check.modelAnswer: A nucleus that holds the DNA and is enclosed by its own membrane.

check.stem: Name the four eukaryotic groups covered by this course.
A classmate sorts organisms into 'single-celled' versus 'many-celled' and calls the first pile prokaryotes. Explain the flaw in that sorting.
check.modelAnswer: The piles confuse body design with cell plan: several protoctists and the yeast fungus are single cells yet carry an enclosed nucleus, which makes them eukaryotes, while some prokaryotes can cling together in clumps without becoming many-celled organisms.

check.stem: A pond sample yields an organism that is one cell, about twice the length of a bacterium, and clearly shows a rounded structure enclosed by a double membrane. Which camp does it belong to, and what additional observation would tell you which of the four groups it sits in?
check.modelAnswer: It is a eukaryote because its genetic material sits in a membrane-enclosed nucleus; grouping it further needs observations such as chloroplasts (plant-like), a chitin-based hyphal or yeast form (fungus), feeding by ingesting or absorbing, or none of those (protoctist).

lessons.title: Animals, plants, fungi and protoctists: the four feature lists
lessons.opening: Animals and plants are the two many-celled groups most people picture first, and their feature lists overlap more than students expect. Both are built from cells with enclosed nuclei, yet each carries a small set of traits the other lacks. Learning the pairs of contrasts — walls, chloroplasts, carbohydrate stores and feeding — earns the marks.
keyPoints: Animal cells have a surrounding membrane, an enclosed nucleus, mitochondria and no cell wall.
Animal bodies are many-celled and their carbohydrate store is glycogen.
Plant cells add a cell wall built with cellulose and chloroplasts that harvest light for photosynthesis.
Plant bodies are many-celled and their carbohydrate store is starch.

low.restatement: Animals: many cells, nucleus with its own membrane, no cell wall, glycogen as the store. Plants: the same core plan plus cellulose walls and chloroplasts, storing starch.
low.analogy: Think of two flats with identical heating (mitochondria) but only one installed with solar panels (chloroplasts) and reinforced outer walls (cellulose).
low.examPointer: Two-mark versions of this question usually want one animal-only feature and one plant-only feature — a wall with cellulose, chloroplasts, or starch versus the glycogen store.

medium.restatement: The contrasts that separate the two groups are structural (wall, chloroplast) and biochemical (starch versus glycogen storage), while nucleus, membrane and mitochondria stay common.
medium.analogy: Two factories may run the same power supply yet stock different warehouses: plants bank starch behind cellulose walls, animals bank glycogen in unwalled units.
medium.examPointer: When a question shows an unlabelled cell diagram, walls and chloroplasts identify plant cells; their absence with mitochondria visible points to animal material.

check.stem: Which combination correctly lists a plant-only feature and an animal-only feature?

options.text: Cellulose cell wall — glycogen carbohydrate store
options.explanation: Walls with cellulose belong to plants; glycogen storage belongs to animals.

options.text: Chloroplasts — cellulose cell wall
options.explanation: Both features sit on the plant side of the comparison.
options.misconception: two plant traits labelled as the animal pair

options.text: Glycogen store — mitochondria present
options.explanation: Mitochondria appear in both groups, so they cannot separate them.

options.text: Nucleus with its own membrane — starch store
options.explanation: The enclosed nucleus is common to both groups; starch belongs to plants.

check.stem: A stained slide shows cells with visible chloroplasts and a thin outer wall. Which group do they come from?

options.text: Protoctists
options.explanation: Some protoctists photosynthesise, but the combination with a cellulose wall matches the plant list here.

options.text: Plants
options.explanation: Chloroplasts plus a wall is the classic plant-cell pairing.

options.text: Animals
options.explanation: Animal cells never carry chloroplasts or walls.

options.text: Fungi
options.explanation: Fungal walls are not built with cellulose and the group has no chloroplasts.

check.stem: Which statement about carbohydrate storage is correct for these two groups?

options.text: Both groups bank starch
options.explanation: Animal cells store carbohydrate as glycogen instead.

options.text: Neither group stores carbohydrate
options.explanation: Both groups maintain a carbohydrate reserve.

options.text: Plants bank starch; animals bank glycogen
options.explanation: The note names starch for plants and glycogen for animals.

options.text: Plants bank glycogen; animals bank starch
options.explanation: The two stores have been swapped.

check.stem: What do animal cells and plant cells BOTH possess?

options.text: A cellulose wall and chloroplasts
options.explanation: Those belong to plant cells only.

options.text: Chloroplasts but no mitochondria
options.explanation: Plant cells contain mitochondria alongside their chloroplasts.

options.text: A cellulose wall but no nucleus
options.explanation: Both groups are eukaryotic, so nuclei are present in both.

options.text: A nucleus enclosed by its own membrane and mitochondria
options.explanation: Both groups run the core eukaryotic plan including mitochondria.

check.stem: Why is the absence of a cell wall a reliable marker for animal cells in this course?

options.text: Because plant cells carry a cellulose wall and fungal cells are walled too, while animal cells run without one
options.explanation: The wall contrast separates animal cells from both other many-celled groups.

options.text: Because animal cells are always spherical
options.explanation: Shape varies across animal tissues.

options.text: Because animal cells cannot survive with a wall
options.explanation: The note never claims walls harm animal cells.

options.text: Because walls appear only in single-celled organisms
options.explanation: Plant bodies are many-celled with walls on every cell.

check.stem: List three structures an animal cell has that the note names, besides the nucleus.
State the material that plant cell walls are built from and the plant carbohydrate store.
check.modelAnswer: Walls are built from cellulose, and the store is starch.

check.stem: Explain why chloroplasts let plants count as self-feeders while animals must find food.
check.modelAnswer: Chloroplasts capture light energy and drive photosynthesis, so a plant can manufacture the sugars it needs from simple raw materials, whereas animal cells carry no chloroplasts and must take in ready-made organic food.

check.stem: A food label lists a carbohydrate reserve harvested from an unknown organism. Chemical tests show the reserve is glycogen. Which of the two groups did the organism belong to, and which organelle would you expect its cells to contain for releasing energy from that reserve?
check.modelAnswer: Glycogen points to the animal group, since plants bank starch; its cells would contain mitochondria to release energy from the stored carbohydrate.

lessons.title: Fungi and protoctists: the often-confused pair
lessons.opening: Fungi and protoctists are the two groups candidates mix up most often. Fungi build bodies of thread-like hyphae, may be single-celled like yeast, and absorb food from their surroundings. Protoctists are the leftovers drawer of the classification: a very varied set of mostly single-celled organisms that fit none of the other three lists.
keyPoints: Multicellular fungi are built from hyphae, which are thread-like filaments carrying many nuclei.
Some fungi are single-celled, and yeast is the named example.
Protoctists form a very varied set whose members share no single defining trait beyond being eukaryotic.
Drawing and labelling fungal and protoctist cells is an explicitly named exam skill.

low.restatement: Fungi: hyphae threads, sometimes single cells such as yeast. Protoctists: a varied catch-all group of mostly microscopic eukaryotes.
low.analogy: If the classification were a block of flats, fungi would be the identical floor plan repeated along corridors, protoctists the odds-and-ends storage rooms.
low.examPointer: Practise sketching a labelled fungal cell and two contrasting protoctist cells — the note flags exactly this drawing skill.

medium.restatement: Fungal bodies are hyphal networks whose walls carry no cellulose and no chloroplasts ever appear; protoctist diversity means identification relies on ruling out the other groups' defining features.
medium.analogy: Fungi are a standardised building system; protoctists are a lost-property office — you identify an item by failing to match it to any other department.
medium.examPointer: If asked to justify a protoctist assignment, argue from elimination: not an animal, not a plant, not a fungus.

check.stem: Which structure builds the bodies of multicellular fungi?

options.text: Thread-like hyphae containing many nuclei
options.explanation: The note describes hyphae as the thread-like building units of multicellular fungi.

options.text: Cellulose leaves and stems
options.explanation: That is plant anatomy.

options.text: Muscle and nerve tissues
options.explanation: Those are animal tissues.

options.text: Free-floating colonies of identical single cells only
options.explanation: Multicellular fungi are hyphal, not loose cell colonies.

check.stem: Which fungus is named as the single-celled example?

options.text: Plasmodium
options.explanation: That is a protoctist.

options.text: Yeast
options.explanation: The note names yeast as the single-celled fungus.

options.text: Mucor
options.explanation: Mucor is the named multicellular genus.

options.text: Lactobacillus
options.explanation: That is a bacterium, not a fungus.

check.stem: Why does the protoctist group resist a one-line definition?

options.text: Because they have no nuclei
options.explanation: Protoctists are eukaryotes with enclosed nuclei.

options.text: Because they are all parasitic
options.explanation: The note gives no such blanket claim.

options.text: Because its members are too varied to share one distinguishing trait beyond the eukaryotic plan
options.explanation: The note calls the group very diverse with features differing from the other three groups.

options.text: Because all protoctists are photosynthetic
options.explanation: Only some are; the group is not uniform.

check.stem: A diagram shows a cell with a wall, an enclosed nucleus, mitochondria and no chloroplasts, growing as a thread of connected compartments. Best match?

options.text: A plant leaf cell
options.explanation: Leaf cells carry chloroplasts.

options.text: A bacterial cell
options.explanation: Bacteria lack the enclosed nucleus.

options.text: An animal skin cell
options.explanation: Animal cells have neither walls nor hyphal threading.

options.text: A fungal cell from a hypha
options.explanation: Wall plus enclosed nucleus, mitochondria, no chloroplasts, hyphal thread — the fungal portrait.

check.stem: Which exam skill does the note explicitly flag for fungi and protoctists?

options.text: Recognising, drawing and labelling their cells from images
options.explanation: The closing hint names practising labelled drawings of fungal and protoctist cells.

options.text: Measuring their generation times in culture
options.explanation: No growth-rate work appears in this note.

options.text: Calculating their surface-area-to-volume ratios
options.explanation: That belongs to transport notes, not this one.

options.text: Staining them with iodine to test for starch
options.explanation: Iodine testing is a food-test technique, not a classification skill.

check.stem: Give the word for the thread-like filaments that build multicellular fungi.
check.modelAnswer: Hyphae — thread-like filaments packed with nuclei.

check.stem: Name one single-celled fungus and one disease-causing protoctist mentioned across this topic.
check.modelAnswer: Yeast is the single-celled fungus; Plasmodium is the malaria protoctist.

check.stem: Explain why a yeast cell counts as a fungus rather than as a protoctist.
check.modelAnswer: Yeast carries the fungal toolkit — a wall, an enclosed nucleus and no chloroplasts — and it reproduces and feeds the fungal way, so it is placed with fungi even though it lives as a single cell; protoctists are identified only after the three defined groups have been ruled out.

check.stem: A new microscope sample shows a many-celled organism built from branching threads with walls, several nuclei per compartment and no chloroplasts. Assign it to a group and justify the assignment with two features.
check.modelAnswer: It belongs with the fungi: the branching thread construction matches hyphae, and the combination of walls with no chloroplasts plus many nuclei per compartment is the fungal portrait rather than the plant one.

glossary.definition: An organism whose cells keep their DNA inside a nucleus enclosed by its own membrane.
One of the thread-like filaments, packed with nuclei, that builds the body of a multicellular fungus.
A varied eukaryotic organism that fits none of the animal, plant or fungal feature lists.
The plant organelle that harvests light energy to drive photosynthesis.
